## Local Volatility Models

In [[quantitative-finance|mathematical finance]] **local volatility models**
are option pricing models that treat volatility as a function of both the
asset price $S_t$ and time $t$. The asset price process $(S_t)$ has dynamics
given by the [[stochastic-differential-equations|SDE]]

$$
dS_t=(r_t-d_t)S_t\,dt+\sigma(t,S_t)S_t\,dW_t,
$$

where $r_t$ is the interest rate, $d_t$ the dividend yield and $W$ a
[[brownian-motion|Brownian motion]]. A derivation as for the
[[black-scholes-merton-model|Black-Scholes PDE]] shows that if
$V_t=u(t,S_t)$ is the value of the replicating portfolio then

$$
\partial_tu+rx\,\partial_xu+\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2(t,x)x^2\,\partial_{xx}u-ru=0.
$$

Solving this PDE is inefficient for pricing a single option, since it requires
the solution at all $(t,x)$ just to produce one number.

## Dupire's PDE

In the local volatility model there is a model-dependent result, [[dupires-formula|Dupire's
formula]], that gives call prices directly as a function of maturity and
strike. Let $C(T,K)$ be the price at time $0$ of a call with maturity $T$ and
strike $K$, and take constant $r$ and no dividends. Then

$$
\frac{\partial C}{\partial T}(T,K)=-rK\frac{\partial C}{\partial K}(T,K)
+\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2(T,K)K^2\frac{\partial^2C}{\partial K^2}(T,K),
$$

with the natural initial condition $C(0,K)=(S_0-K)_+$, since at $T=0$ the
option price is the immediate payoff. The equation can be read backwards to
recover the local volatility from option prices,

$$
\sigma^2(T,K)=\frac{\partial_TC+rK\,\partial_KC}{\tfrac{1}{2}K^2\,\partial_{KK}C},
$$

which also yields the implied volatility surface $I(T,K)$ of the model (see
[[volatility-surfaces]]).

## The CEV Model

A special case is the **constant elasticity of variance (CEV) model**, with
dynamics

$$
dS_t=\mu S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t^{\gamma}\,dW_t,
$$

where $\sigma>0$ and $\gamma\ge 0$ is the **elasticity** parameter. This is a
local volatility model with $\sigma(t,x)=\sigma x^{\gamma-1}$, so the
instantaneous variance of returns is $\sigma^2S_t^{2(\gamma-1)}$, whose
elasticity with respect to $S_t$ is constant. Special cases are

- $\gamma=1$: [[geometric-brownian-motion]], the Black-Scholes-Merton model,
- $\gamma=0$: the arithmetic (Bachelier) model $dS_t=\mu S_t\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t$.

For $\gamma<1$ volatility rises when the price falls (the **leverage
effect**), which produces a downward-sloping implied volatility skew, as is
observed in equity markets. For $\gamma>1$ the skew is upward-sloping.

## Problems

A local volatility model is designed to produce an implied volatility surface
$I(T,K)$ that is not flat in $T$ or $K$, but it is still imperfect. It suffers
from the so-called $(t,T,K)$-problem.

Since $\sigma=\sigma(t,x)$, volatility is always the same given the same time
and stock price. If we calibrate at time $0$ and obtain the surface $I(0,T,K)$
from options maturing at $T$, we therefore expect the same surface
$I(t,T+t,K)$ at a later time $t$ from options maturing at $T+t$. Empirically,
these two implied volatility surfaces are not the same under time
translation, which contradicts the model. This motivates
[[stochastic-volatility-model|stochastic volatility models]].
